01The memory hierarchy — where the time actually goes

Latency of a single access at each level. The right column pretends one CPU cycle = one second, so you can feel a gap that's otherwise too fast to imagine.

registers<1 KB

System cachetens of MB

DRAM128 GB
~425 cyc

A register is now; RAM is a 7-minute warehouse trip; the SSD is like mail-ordering the data and waiting almost four days. Every cache exists to keep you near the top of this list.

02The cache cliffs, drawn by a stopwatch

Pointer-chase latency as the working set grows. Each cliff is a cache running out of room — the chip's memory hierarchy, with no spec sheet.

An L1 hit costs 4 cycles; a DRAM miss ~425 — over 100× worse. Real programs spend much of their life on this curve, which is why "is my data in cache?" usually matters more than the algorithm.

04CPU core scaling

Integer throughput vs threads. Flatlines at 18 — the physical core count, made visible.

Peak 318 G/s — 15× one core (not 18×: E-cores are slower & share a power budget).

05Memory bandwidth saturates early

Streaming GB/s as cores pile on. One core already pulls a third of the whole bus.

Maxed by ~6 cores. Compute scales to 18; bandwidth doesn't — the practical line between "more cores help" and "more cores are wasted."

109× slower. Identical data, identical size — only the order changed. The prefetcher hides latency only when it can predict you.

Predictable order ≈ free; a coin-flip branch costs ~3×. The predictor learns patterns — even alternating — and only random truly defeats it.

One core. Integer ops per cycle, then floating-point.

A 128-bit register holds 4 numbers; one instruction adds all four. Lanes × units = a 2.8× jump on top of everything else.

09The hidden cache (TLB)

Same 128 KB of data, in L1 both times — but spread across 1024 pages vs packed. Cycles/access.

packed
 
3.8
spread
131
131

30× slower to read the same in-cache data — because translating the address overflowed the TLB. A second, hidden cache for addresses, and you can blow it too.

10Disk — bigger reads, less overhead

Reading the same 512 MB, by block size. Every read is a system call with fixed cost.

~100× faster from block size alone — amortizing the syscall over more bytes. Random access stays brutal: 71 µs (~315,000 cycles).

11GPU needs thousands of threads

FP32 throughput vs threads launched. Below ~250k it's idle — slower than the CPU.

Peak 14.9 TFLOP/s — but it must be fed. A GPU hides latency with sheer numbers, not the CPU's cleverness.

12Two processors, two philosophies of hiding latency

CPU · 18 cores

Hides latency with cleverness — out-of-order execution, branch prediction, prefetch. Fast even on a single thread.

1.9 TFLOP/s  ·  300 GB/s
GPU · 40 cores

Hides latency with sheer numbers — ~5,000 lanes, thousands of threads. Below ~250k threads it's slower than the CPU; above, ~8× faster.

14.9 TFLOP/s  ·  578 GB/s

★It all comes down to two knobs

independence

Is there other work to overlap while you wait? A dependency chain pins you to 1×; independent work buys ~6–20×. It showed up in every test — dependent vs independent adds, instruction layout, streaming loads, the FMA ceiling.

locality

Is the data reachable cheaply? Up to ~100× between L1 and a random DRAM miss, and the prefetcher erases the size penalty entirely when your access pattern is predictable.

Multiply them and you span ~2,000× between best-case compute and a random DRAM miss — ~300,000× down to the SSD. Which end your program lands on is decided mostly by data layout and access order, not how many instructions you write.

Measured on this machine with timed loops — no spec sheets, no system APIs reporting the answer.
